response_text: Round-robin maps naturally to a FIFO ready queue of TCB pointers. The kernel always runs the TCB at the front of the ready queue. When that thread calls yield (cooperative lab) the kernel saves its context, dequeues its TCB from the front, and if it is still READY enqueues it at the back. The new front element becomes the next running thread. If a thread blocks (e.g., on I/O/semaphore), its TCB is removed from the ready queue entirely; when it unblocks, the TCB is pushed to the back to preserve fairness. Compared with a plain array plus a modulo index, a ready queue (implemented as a fixed-size ring buffer of TCB pointers) keeps operations strictly O(1) and avoids “holes,” validity flags, or scans after threads block/exit. It also expresses the policy directly (“front runs → goes to back”), which simplifies edge cases and makes extensions straightforward: per-priority multiple ready queues (one FIFO per priority), and clean sleep/wake by moving TCBs between lists. Arrays are fine for very small systems, but a queue yields clearer invariants and fewer bookkeeping bugs without sacrificing determinism.\n
